title: What Really Happened At Midway: The Battle That Changed The Pacific War
sources: Naval History and Heritage Command (history.navy.mil): Battle of Midway; Recollections of Lt. George Gay (oral history)
NAVSEA: Battle of Midway (Yorktown restored in 72 hours); Britannica: Battle of Midway
Parshall & Tully, Shattered Sword (2005) on the 'five minutes' claim; Fuchida's postwar account
USNI Naval History Jun 2017 'Torpedo Eight's Celebrated Survivor' (Gay = only survivor of the 30 who flew from Hornet)
Footage: The Battle of Midway (1942, John Ford, US Navy, public domain); NHHC photos (US Navy, public domain)
Hedged in script: codebreakers read 'only pieces'; casualties 'about' 3,000 / 300; Best's bomb 'very likely'; Ford wounded by a fragment (his account)

beats.text: On the morning of June the fourth, 1942, four Japanese aircraft carriers were sailing toward a tiny island in the middle of the Pacific.

v.q: The Battle of Midway 1942 John Ford

beats.text: By that evening, all four were burning.
The films tell it as a miracle. A lucky dive at the perfect second, five minutes before Japan would have won.
The real story is stranger. It was won by a fake message about drinking water, a ship that should not have been there, and a pilot who followed a single wake across the sea.
Six months earlier, Japan had struck Pearl Harbor. Since then, it had not lost a single major battle.
Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto wanted to finish the job. He would take Midway and lure the surviving American carriers out to be destroyed.
Midway was a small atoll, two little islands and a lagoon, about thirteen hundred miles from Hawaii.
But it was the last American outpost before Pearl Harbor itself.
Yamamoto sent a huge force. Carriers, battleships, transports, and a strike at Alaska to pull eyes away.
At the heart of it were four carriers under Admiral Chuichi Nagumo. Akagi, Kaga, Soryu and Hiryu. Four of the six that had hit Pearl Harbor.
He expected to surprise the Americans. Instead, the Americans were waiting for him.
In a windowless basement at Pearl Harbor, a team of codebreakers worked around the clock. Their leader was Commander Joseph Rochefort.
Films often show them reading Japan's plans like a newspaper. In reality, they could read only pieces of each message.
And one piece kept coming back. The next target was called AF. But where was AF?
Rochefort was sure AF meant Midway. Some officers in Washington were not. A wrong guess could lose the war in the Pacific.
So his team set a trap. Midway was told to send a message in plain language, saying its water plant had broken down.

v.text: OUR WATER PLANT HAS BROKEN DOWN

beats.text: Soon the codebreakers picked up a Japanese report. AF, it said, was short of water.
Now Admiral Chester Nimitz knew where. And from the pieces, roughly when.
But knowing was not enough. He had only three carriers to bring. And one of them was badly damaged.
USS Yorktown had been hit a month earlier in the Coral Sea. Repairs were expected to take weeks.

v.q: USS Yorktown dry dock Pearl Harbor May 1942

beats.text: Nimitz gave the yard three days. Workers swarmed her day and night, and in about seventy-two hours, Yorktown sailed.
Japan believed Yorktown was out of the war. That was the ship that should not have been there.

v.text: THE SHIP THAT SHOULDN'T BE THERE

beats.text: There was one more problem. Admiral Halsey, the most famous carrier commander, was in hospital with a painful skin disease.
He picked a quiet cruiser admiral to replace him. Raymond Spruance had never commanded carriers in battle.
On the island, a Hollywood director was waiting too. Commander John Ford of the Navy had come with a small film camera.

v.q: The Battle of Midway 1942 John Ford

beats.text: Before dawn on June the fourth, a patrol plane found the Japanese fleet.
At six thirty, more than a hundred Japanese planes hit Midway.

v.q: The Battle of Midway 1942 John Ford

beats.text: Ford kept filming as bombs fell. He was hit in the arm by a fragment and kept going. Some of that shaking film is what you are seeing now.

v.q: The Battle of Midway 1942 John Ford

beats.text: Midway's own fighters were old and outclassed. Most of them were shot down or wrecked.
Bombers from the island attacked the carriers next. They scored no hits. But they kept Nagumo under pressure all morning.
Then his strike leader radioed. Midway needed a second attack.
Nagumo had planes waiting, armed with torpedoes in case American ships appeared. He ordered them switched to bombs for the island.
Then a late scout plane reported something he did not expect. American ships. Then, an American carrier.
Now he had to recover his returning planes, rearm again, and fight. All at once.
Spruance, meanwhile, made the boldest call of the day. He launched early, at long range, to catch the Japanese with planes on deck.
The first Americans to arrive were the slow torpedo bombers.
Torpedo Squadron Eight, from Hornet, found the carriers alone. Fifteen planes, no fighter cover.
Japanese fighters cut them down one after another. Not one torpedo hit.
Of the thirty men who flew, only one lived. Ensign George Gay, floating in the sea, hiding under a seat cushion.
More torpedo squadrons came in and were shot to pieces too.
Their sacrifice was real. Their attacks pulled Japanese fighters down to sea level, and kept the carriers turning and busy.
High above, almost no one was watching the sky.
Lieutenant Commander Wade McClusky was leading Enterprise's dive bombers. He had searched past the point where the fleet should be. Fuel was running low.
Then he saw a lone Japanese destroyer, racing north at full speed.
It had stayed behind to hunt an American submarine. Now it was running to catch up with the fleet.
McClusky followed its wake. It led him straight to the carriers.
At about twenty past ten, his bombers tipped over and dived.
At almost the same moment, Yorktown's dive bombers arrived from another direction. Nobody had planned it to the minute.
Kaga took several bombs. Soryu was hit by Yorktown's planes and was soon an inferno.
Lieutenant Dick Best and two wingmen went for Akagi, Nagumo's flagship.
One bomb, very likely Best's own, smashed into the hangar, among fuelled and armed planes.
In about six minutes, three of Japan's best carriers were finished.
Here the films usually add their famous line. Five more minutes, and Japan's planes would have launched.

v.q: The Battle of Midway 1942 John Ford

beats.text: That came from Mitsuo Fuchida, a Japanese officer on Akagi, who wrote it after the war.
Historians Jonathan Parshall and Anthony Tully checked the Japanese records. The strike was nowhere near ready. Decks were busy with fighters.
So it was not five minutes of luck. Japan was already losing the race, because of choices made hours earlier.
One Japanese carrier was still untouched. Hiryu.
Her admiral, Tamon Yamaguchi, struck back fast. Her dive bombers followed the Americans home and found Yorktown.
Three bombs hit. Fires broke out. Yet within hours, Yorktown's crew had her moving again.
So when Hiryu's torpedo planes came, they thought she was a second, undamaged carrier.
Two torpedoes hit. Yorktown rolled over to one side, and the crew was ordered to abandon ship.
That afternoon, American dive bombers found Hiryu. Four bombs, and the last carrier was burning.
Yamaguchi chose to stay aboard. He went down with his ship.
That night, Spruance made his second great choice. He turned his carriers away, instead of chasing into the dark.
Yamamoto's battleships were out there, hoping for a night fight the Americans would have lost. The trap closed on empty sea.
Yorktown did not give up easily. She stayed afloat for two more days, until a Japanese submarine finished her.
By then the cruiser Mikuma had also been sunk, and Yamamoto had called the invasion off.
The cost was heavy on both sides. Japan lost four carriers and about three thousand men. America lost Yorktown, a destroyer, and about three hundred men.

v.q: The Battle of Midway 1942 John Ford

beats.text: Japan would never again choose where the war in the Pacific was fought.
So what happened to them after?

v.q: The Battle of Midway 1942 John Ford

beats.text: George Gay spent hours in the water and was picked up by a patrol plane the next day. He lived to tell the story for the rest of his life.
Dick Best never flew in combat again. A faulty oxygen system made him sick, and doctors found tuberculosis.
Joseph Rochefort was moved away from codebreaking after quarrels in Washington. He was sent to run a floating dry dock.
He got his medal only in 1986, long after his death.
And Yamamoto? Less than a year later, American codebreakers read his travel plans. His plane was shot down over the jungle.
John Ford turned his footage into a short Navy film. It won an Oscar.

v.q: The Battle of Midway 1942 John Ford

beats.text: So how true is the movie version? The courage is true. The sacrifice is true. The timing really was razor thin.
But Midway was not a miracle. It was a codebreaker's trap, a ship repaired in three days, and a pilot who trusted a single wake.
If you want the true story behind the next big war film, subscribe. The real history is always stranger.

v.q: The Battle of Midway 1942 John Ford
